# Stdlib Type-Surface Style Contract

Source: https://github.com/hew-lang/hew/blob/main/docs/stdlib-style-contract.md

# Stdlib Type-Surface Style Contract

> **Audience:** anyone writing or reviewing a stdlib module (`std/**/*.hew`).

---

## Why this contract exists

v0.5 adopts an explicit-width-only integer naming policy. The `int` and `uint`
aliases (formerly compiler aliases for `i64` and `u64`) are removed. Stdlib
modules must use explicit widths on all public surfaces, removing the ambiguity
that led readers to assume Go/Swift platform-sized semantics.

---

## The invariants

### 1. Public API integer width

Every `pub fn` parameter, return type, trait-method signature, and struct field
**must** use an explicit-width integer:

- Signed: `i8`, `i16`, `i32`, `i64`
- Unsigned: `u8`, `u16`, `u32`, `u64`
- Platform-sized (pointer math only): `isize`, `usize`

The removed aliases `int` / `Int` / `uint` are **not valid type names** and will
produce a compile error with a suggestion to use `i64` or `isize`.

Choose `i64` by default for general-purpose integer values. Choose `usize` for
collection lengths and indices. Choose narrower widths only when the external
ABI requires it (e.g. C errno is `i32`, file descriptors are `i32`).

### 2. Internal ABI seams

`i32`/`i64` inside `extern "C" { ... }` blocks must match the runtime symbol
table exactly. Narrowing casts at the call site (`x as i32`) happen inside
`unsafe`, not in the public signature:

```hew
pub fn len(dq: Deque) -> i64 { unsafe { hew_deque_len(dq) } }

extern "C" {
    fn hew_deque_len(dq: Deque) -> i64;
}
```

### 3. Fallible conversion

The sole parse-to-integer shape is:

```hew
pub fn string_to_int(s: string) -> i64 { ... }
```

No sentinel returns (`-1` meaning "missing"). Express absence with
`Option<i64>` or `Result<i64, E>`.

### 4. Handle lifetime

Handle types must expose `close()` and/or `free()` as explicit trait methods.
Automatic drop is permitted, but the explicit release API must also exist.

### 5. Naming convention

Fallible variants are named `try_*`. Non-fallible variants either panic or
return a documented default. Dual variants come in pairs (`read`/`try_read`).

### 6. Wire annotations

`#[wire]`-annotated types use explicit-width integer fields. Choose the width
that matches the schema contract — `i64` for general counters, narrower widths
only when the wire protocol requires them.

---

## Canonical example

```hew
trait DequeMethods {
    fn push_front(dq: Deque, value: i64);
    fn pop_front(dq: Deque) -> i64;
    fn len(dq: Deque) -> i64;
}

impl DequeMethods for Deque {
    fn push_front(dq: Deque, value: i64) { unsafe { hew_deque_push_front(dq, value) }; }
    fn pop_front(dq: Deque) -> i64 { unsafe { hew_deque_pop_front(dq) } }
    fn len(dq: Deque) -> i64 { unsafe { hew_deque_len(dq) } }
}

extern "C" {
    fn hew_deque_push_front(dq: Deque, value: i64);
    fn hew_deque_pop_front(dq: Deque) -> i64;
    fn hew_deque_len(dq: Deque) -> i64;
}
```

---

## Migration from `int`

If you encounter `int` or `uint` in a `.hew` file, replace with `i64` or `u64`
respectively. The compiler will suggest the replacement:

```
error: unknown type `int`; use `i64` for fixed 64-bit integers or `isize` for
       pointer-sized integers
```

The `scripts/lint-stdlib-int-surface.sh` script may still reference the old
`int` surface contract — it should be updated or removed.

---

# Troubleshooting

Source: https://github.com/hew-lang/hew/blob/main/docs/troubleshooting.md

# Troubleshooting

This guide is a short checklist for common `hew` compiler, CLI, and source-build failures.

Start with the smallest command that still reproduces the problem:

```sh
hew check path/to/main.hew
hew compile path/to/main.hew
```

For multi-file compile/typecheck flows, `hew check` and `hew compile` operate
on a single entry-point file and resolve imports recursively from there. Pass
`main.hew` (or your real top-level entry file), not every file in the tree.

For the standard bootstrap flow, start with `adze init <name>` so you get
`hew.toml`, `main.hew`, and `.gitignore`, then begin with
`hew check main.hew` / `hew compile main.hew`. `hew init` remains the lighter
source-only scaffold: it writes `main.hew` plus `README.md`, but no
`hew.toml`.

## Build & linking

Common signs:

- `Error: clang not found. Install LLVM to link Hew programs.`
- raw linker output after `hew compile <file.hew>`
- `hew check <file.hew>` succeeds, but `hew compile ...` fails

What to check:

- Use `hew check <file.hew>` first to separate frontend failures from
  link/toolchain failures.
- Hew forwards raw linker output. Fix missing libraries, bad `--link-lib`
  flags, or target mismatches before chasing compiler internals.
- For this repo, use `make`, `make release`, `make test`, and other Makefile
  targets instead of calling Cargo directly.
- Use the toolchain from the root README: Rust stable and LLVM 22.
- On macOS, use Homebrew LLVM (`LLVM_PREFIX="$(brew --prefix llvm)"`) so
  `llvm-sys` can locate the static libraries.
- After switching LLVM installs or `CC` / `CXX`, run
  `make clean` before rebuilding.
- If the program builds but you need a debugger, use
  `hew debug <file.hew> [-- args...]`.

## Type errors & type inference

Common signs:

- a `type mismatch` error such as `expected i64, found string`
- `cannot infer type`
- `return type mismatch: expected ..., found ...`

What to check:

- Start with `hew check <file.hew>`.
- While iterating on the same file or directory,
  `hew watch <file_or_dir>` can keep rerunning checks automatically on every
  save — see [Watch mode](#watch-mode) below.
- Add explicit types to function parameters, return values, locals flowing into
  generic code, and any `_` placeholders.
- `type Foo = _;` currently fails closed with `cannot infer type for type alias`
  and a help suggestion to add a type annotation.
- `fn ... -> _` and trait default methods with bodies and `-> _` fail closed
  too: if the checker cannot resolve a concrete return type, Hew reports an
  inference error at the checker/output boundary instead of guessing later in
  serialization or codegen.
- When you hit a mismatch, fix the earliest ambiguous binding or return value,
  not only the final call site.

## Module & import resolution

Common signs:

- a module-not-found error for a local or package module
- a `cannot resolve import ...` diagnostic
- an `unused import: ...` warning while reorganizing imports

What to check:

- Run `hew check <file.hew>` or `hew compile <file.hew>` against the real
  entry file, not a peer file inside a module directory.
- For `import greeting;`, Hew looks for `greeting.hew` beside the importer or
  `greeting/greeting.hew` in a directory-form module. The entry file stem must
  match the directory name.
- Other top-level `.hew` files in that directory merge into the same module
  automatically. Subdirectories do not; import child modules explicitly, for
  example `import text_stats::words;`.
- Standard library imports are available under the last path segment:
  `import std::fs;` gives `fs`, and `import std::encoding::json;` gives `json`.
- Search roots are tried in this exact order, first match wins:
  1. `HEWPATH` (colon-separated entries; each entry is the parent directory of
     `std/`)
  2. `HEW_STD` (the path to `std/` itself; Hew uses its parent as the search
     root)
  3. the installed `<prefix>/share/hew` tree relative to the `hew` binary
  4. a development fallback to the repo root when `std/` exists two levels
     above the binary
- `hew.toml` does not configure module search paths. Use `HEWPATH` or
  `HEW_STD` when you need Hew to look in a non-default module root.
- If the missing module is a package dependency, run `adze install`. If it is
  undeclared in project metadata, add it with `adze add ...` first.
- Use the candidate-path list in the module-not-found error to confirm where Hew
  actually looked.
- `import mod::*;` works, but wildcard imports currently can emit a
  false-positive `unused import` warning when the module is only used through
  type references. Prefer bare (`import mod;`) or selective
  (`import mod::{Name}`) imports while reorganizing modules.
- To browse the shipped stdlib, generate docs for it directly:

  ```sh
  hew doc std/ --output-dir doc/std
  ```

  This is the recommended discovery workflow today; `hew doc --list` does not
  exist.

See also:
[`../examples/directory_module_demo/README.md`](../examples/directory_module_demo/README.md),
[`../examples/multifile/README.md`](../examples/multifile/README.md), and
[`specs/HEW-SPEC-2026.md`](specs/HEW-SPEC-2026.md).

## Pattern matching & exhaustiveness

Common signs:

- `non-exhaustive match: missing Blue`
- the same kind of error when a `match` on `Option<T>` skips `None`
- the same kind of error when a `match` on `Result<T, E>` skips `Ok` or `Err`

What to check:

- Matches over enums, `Option<T>`, `Result<T, E>`, machine states, and `bool`
  are fail-closed: cover every case or add `_ => ...`.
- For scalar or open-ended values such as `i64`, a missing catch-all is only a
  warning.
- When a new variant or state lands, update old match sites before chasing
  downstream type errors.
- For machine-specific transition and exhaustiveness rules, see
  [`specs/MACHINE-SPEC.md`](specs/MACHINE-SPEC.md).

## Mutability & variable bindings

Common signs:

- a `cannot assign to immutable variable` error
- a `variable ... is already defined in this scope` error
- a warning that a variable shadows a binding in an outer scope

What to check:

- `let` bindings are immutable. Change a binding to `var` only when
  reassignment is actually intended.
- Same-scope rebinding is an error. Rename the second binding instead of
  treating it like reassignment.
- Nested-scope shadowing is a warning for locals, but it can be a hard error
  when it would shadow synthetic bindings such as actor fields.
- Prefix intentionally unused or intentionally shadowed names with `_` to
  suppress noise.

## Function calls & arity

Common signs:

- an `undefined function` error
- `cannot find value ... in this scope` / `cannot find type ... in this scope`
- `this function takes N argument(s) but M were supplied`

What to check:

- Fix spelling first. Hew can suggest close matches for values, functions,
  types, and fields.
- Re-check whether the call should stay qualified under a module
  (`utils.helper()`) or be brought into scope by a selective import.
- Recount arguments after refactors, especially when constructors or helper
  signatures changed.

## Wire type validation

Common signs:

- an `error: removed required field ...` compatibility failure
- `wire check: 1 error(s), 0 warning(s)`

What to check:

- Compare the current schema against a baseline with
  `hew wire check <file.hew> --against baseline.hew`.
- Treat field tags as stable IDs. Do not renumber or reuse them.
- Removing required fields, changing a wire declaration from struct to enum (or
  back), or setting `min_version` above the baseline version is breaking.
- Use the last released or otherwise agreed baseline schema, not another
  in-progress branch snapshot.

## Watch mode

`hew watch` re-runs type-checking (and optionally the program) every time a
watched file changes. It uses the same check pipeline as `hew check`, so
all diagnostics appear in the same format.

```sh
hew watch myapp.hew               # Re-check on every save
hew watch --run myapp.hew         # Re-check and re-run on each successful check
hew watch --clear myapp.hew       # Clear terminal before each check
hew watch --debounce 500 myapp.hew  # Wait 500 ms after last event (default: 300)
```

This is the recommended inner-loop workflow for type-error hunts and
refactors. Exit with `Ctrl-C`.

For the full flag reference, see the [Watch mode section of
`../hew-cli/README.md`](../hew-cli/README.md#watch-mode).

## Documentation generation

Common signs:

- `Error: <file>: <message>` on stderr and one or more modules missing from
  the output directory
- `No .hew files found` followed by exit 1
- `No modules to document` followed by exit 1
- `--open` has no visible effect

What to check:

- Files that fail to parse are **skipped**: their errors are printed to stderr,
  but documentation for any valid files in the same run is still written.
  `hew doc` exits 1 after generation if any file had parse errors. Run
  `hew check <file.hew>` on each source file first to identify and fix parse
  errors so all modules appear in the output.
- Parse **warnings** are also printed to stderr, but they do not block
  generation or force a non-zero exit on their own.
- If no output is written and there are no parse errors, confirm that the input
  path exists and contains `.hew` files. `hew doc` does not fall back to the
  current directory — pass at least one file or directory explicitly.
- To browse the stdlib, point `hew doc` at the shipped stdlib tree itself
  (`hew doc std/` from a repo checkout or install tree root).
- `--open` only opens `index.html` after HTML generation. It is silently
  ignored when `--format markdown` is set.
- The output directory (default `./doc`) is created automatically. If creation
  fails (e.g. a permissions issue), the error is printed to stderr and
  `hew doc` exits 1.

- [`../hew-cli/README.md`](../hew-cli/README.md) — CLI command reference
- [`../examples/README.md`](../examples/README.md) — runnable example entry
  points
- [`../examples/directory_module_demo/README.md`](../examples/directory_module_demo/README.md)
  — directory-form modules
- [`../examples/multifile/README.md`](../examples/multifile/README.md) —
  multi-file module patterns

- [`specs/MACHINE-SPEC.md`](specs/MACHINE-SPEC.md) — machine semantics

If you still need help, include the exact `hew` command, the entry-point file
path, the full diagnostic output, `hew version`, and your OS/toolchain details.

# Hew v0.5 Value-Semantics and Ownership Contract

Source: https://github.com/hew-lang/hew/blob/main/docs/v05/ownership.md

# Hew v0.5 Value-Semantics and Ownership Contract

## Core principle: single ownership, move by default

Hew's owned heap types (`string`, `bytes`, `Vec<T>`, `HashMap<K,V>`, and
user-defined types) have exactly one owner at a time. Assigning a binding,
passing an owned value to a function, or sending it to an actor **moves**
it — the source binding becomes invalid, and using it afterward is a
compile-time `use of moved value` error. There is no implicit copy-on-call.

Reaching for a second independent copy is explicit: `val.clone()` (method
form) or `clone val` (prefix form) — see below.

Sending a value to another actor is also a move at the language level, with a
runtime-level optimization for immutable-shareable types (`string`, `bytes`)
— see "Move on send" below.

## `&T` — immutable borrow marker

```hew
fn describe(s: &string) -> string {
    return s;
}
```

`&T` marks a parameter (or return type) as a **non-owning immutable borrow**:

- The callee gets a read-only view into the caller's value.
- No retain/release is performed — the borrow cannot outlive the owner.
- `&T` lowers to `ValueClass::View` in the HIR, exactly as the existing `IntentKind::Read`
  path for call arguments.

**What `&T` is not (v0.5 constraints):**

| Form | Status | Reason |
|------|--------|--------|
| `&T` (immutable borrow) | ✅ Supported | Q320 — read-only view |
| `&mut T` (mutable borrow) | ❌ Not in v0.5 | Q320 — no exclusive-borrow surface yet |
| `&var T` (legacy spelling) | ❌ Parse error | Rejected at the parser |
| Reference cycles via `&T` | ⚠️ Leak risk | Q321 — no cycle collector; avoid cycles |

The parser will reject `&mut T` with a diagnostic. `&var T` is also rejected. These forms
are reserved for future work.

## `.clone()` / `clone x` — explicit copy

`val.clone()` (method form) and `clone val` (prefix form, unary precedence) are
equivalent and are the canonical way to get a second independent copy of an
owned value without consuming the original:

```hew
let a: Vec<i64> = Vec::new();
a.push(1); a.push(2);
let b = clone a;      // == a.clone() — independent copy
b.push(99);
println(a.len());     // 2
println(b.len());     // 3
```

`string`, `Vec<T>`, `HashMap<K,V>`, `HashSet<T>`, and records (via the
`RecordCloneInplace`/`CopyCloneNoop` MIR rewrites) all have a wired copy path
and clone correctly. The `CloneNotYetSupported` diagnostic is a fail-closed
backstop: it fires for a `.clone()` call the checker cannot map to any real
copy path (a type with no clone method at all, or a heap type whose runtime
copy path genuinely isn't wired yet, e.g. `bytes`). It never fires for
already-resolved clones, and it never silently aliases — every unresolved
`.clone()` call is a compile-time error, not a runtime surprise.

## Move on send

When a value crosses an actor boundary — a `receive fn` method call or
`.send()` on a lambda-actor handle — it is **moved**: the sender can no
longer use it.

```hew
let greeting = "hello";
printer.print_message(greeting);
// println(greeting);  // compile error: use of moved value `greeting`
```

At the runtime level the send mechanism is gated by the value's
admissibility class: immutable-shareable owned types (`string`, `bytes`) are
alias-shared by refcount retain (no byte copy, with a copy-on-write fork on
first mutation of a shared buffer); mutable collections (`Vec<T>`,
`HashMap<K,V>`, `HashSet<T>`) are deep-copied into the receiver's per-actor
heap. From the program's perspective both are indistinguishable from
move-then-independent-value — the sender's binding is invalid either way.
Reach for `.clone()` first if you need to keep using the value after
sending it. See HEW-SPEC-2026.md §3.4.4 and §3.7.2 for the full model.

## Equality: structural only (Q322)

`==` in Hew compares **values**, not object identity:

```hew
let a = "hello";
let b = "hello";
a == b  // true — structural equality, always
```

There is no pointer-equality operator. Two distinct heap allocations holding the same bytes
compare equal. This invariant holds even after COW splits a shared buffer.

## Reference cycles (Q321)

Hew v0.5 uses atomic reference counting without a cycle collector. Constructing reference
cycles via `&T` borrows or actor state will cause the involved values to leak (neither the
cycle collector nor weak references exist yet).

**Guideline:** design data structures as DAGs (trees, acyclic graphs). Cycles are a
documented limitation for v0.5; future work will evaluate ORCA-style cycle collection.

## Remaining work

A zero-copy ownership-move fast path for provably-unique, single-recipient
sends of `Linear`/`iso` values is designed but not yet surfaced in edition
2026 — see HEW-SPEC-2026.md §3.7.2. Every other mechanism described above
(move-on-assignment, move-on-send with the alias-share/deep-copy gate,
`.clone()`/`clone x`) is shipped.

---

# Hew WASM Capability Matrix

Source: https://github.com/hew-lang/hew/blob/main/docs/wasm-capability-matrix.md

# Hew WASM Capability Matrix

This document is the **authoritative** source for which Hew features are
available on each WASM target tier.  It is referenced by the type checker
(`hew-types/src/check/types.rs :: WasmUnsupportedFeature`), the runtime stubs
(`hew-runtime/src/lib.rs :: wasm_stubs`), and the spec
(`docs/specs/HEW-SPEC-2026.md §8.0`).

When a feature is listed as **Reject** or **Warn**, the type checker enforces
that disposition at compile time before any code reaches LLVM/WASM codegen.

---

## Target tiers

| Tier | Crate / Target | Use case |
|------|----------------|----------|
| **Tier 1** | `hew-wasm` compiled to `wasm32-unknown-unknown` via `wasm-bindgen` | Browser playground, editor analysis, in-browser type checking |
| **sandbox-vm-export** | `hew-sandbox-wasm` compiled to `wasm32-unknown-unknown` via `wasm-bindgen` | Browser sandbox bytecode export for the educational VM |
| **sandbox-vm** | `hew-sandbox-vm` TypeScript worker | Browser educational sandbox execution for deterministic sequential bytecode |
| **Tier 2** | `hew-runtime` compiled to `wasm32-wasip1` (formerly `wasm32-wasi`) | WASI execution — `hew build --target=wasm32-wasi` |

**Tier 1** is analysis-only: lexer, parser, and type checker only.  It never
executes Hew programs; it only provides diagnostics.

**sandbox-vm-export** sits alongside Tier 1 rather than replacing it.  The
`hew-sandbox-wasm` crate runs parse, type-check, explicit sandbox profile
admission, and deterministic bytecode package emission for browser callers.  It
does not execute Hew programs.

**sandbox-vm** executes admitted sandbox bytecode in a Web Worker.  The current
interpreter covers deterministic sequential code, checked arithmetic, records,
enums, lowered match dispatch, direct monomorphized calls, strings, vectors, an
educational JavaScript `RegExp` subset for curated regex fixtures, the M4
single-threaded actor scheduler (`spawn`, `send`, `receive`, root `ask/reply`,
actor crash hooks, bounded mailboxes, seeded chaos scheduling, and replay via
trace inputs), and the M5 educational coordination subset: bounded in-memory
channels, in-memory stream/sink/duplex handles layered on those channels,
async task spawn/await, structured scopes with cancellation observation at await
and channel boundaries, deterministic `select`, virtual-time timer arms, and
the M6 educational failure-philosophy subset: declarative supervisor specs,
visible child slots, deterministic one-for-one / one-for-all / rest-for-one
restart decisions, virtual-time restart windows, linked exit messages, monitor
notifications, and `#[on(crash)]` observation before supervisor decisions.
M7 adds a machine-readable sandbox stdlib profile, conservative pure/page-I/O
shims, virtual-clock `time.now` / `time.sleep` / `time.deadline` shims, typed
fail-closed diagnostics for unsupported stdlib symbols, and a DOM-free
playground JSON contract for diagnostics, trace views, controls, share links,
lesson virtual files, and trace export.
This is intentionally reduced sandbox semantics rather than production runtime
parity: link-to-dead traps fail closed, monitor-to-dead fires immediately, and
supervisor restart budget exhaustion escalates through typed runtime failures.
Machine runtime parity, file-backed streams, network-backed streams, and broader
host I/O remain fail-closed with structured `unsupported_instruction` runtime
failures for the post-M7/native-runtime milestones.

**Tier 2** is a genuine execution runtime on top of the WASI ABI.  It uses a
single-threaded cooperative actor scheduler and provides a meaningful subset of
the native runtime capabilities.

For CLI eval, `hew eval --target wasm32-wasi <expr>` and
`hew eval --target wasm32-wasi -f <file>` run through Tier 2. Interactive REPL
mode (`hew eval --target wasm32-wasi` with no file or expression) is rejected,
and `--json` is supported only for those non-interactive eval modes.

---

The **Checker disposition** column documents what the type checker emits when
`enable_wasm_target()` is set (i.e., when compiling for Tier 2), or
`WASM-TODO` when a surface is documented as unresolved / not yet checker-gated.

|---------|-------------------|----------------|----------|

| Pattern matching, ADTs, generics | ✅ Pass | Implemented | — |

## Disposition rationale

### ⚠️ Warn (warning-level)

Features in the **Warn** group are architecturally different on the
single-threaded cooperative WASM scheduler, but they still have a meaningful
runtime implementation.

These exist as warnings (not errors) to allow gradual migration: a program can
be partially WASM-compatible and still get useful analysis feedback.

This group includes `sleep`/`sleep_until` and `#[every(duration)]`, which now
have cooperative semantics on WASM: `sleep` parks the actor at the
**message boundary** (not mid-handler), while periodic handlers are delivered
when the host advances the timer queue.  The warning reminds callers that code
after `sleep` in the same receive handler still executes before the actor
parks, and that periodic dispatch depends on `hew_wasm_timer_tick` /
`hew_wasm_sched_tick` driving the queue.

### 🚫 Error (compile-time reject)

Features in the **Error** group are rejected at compile time because wasm32 has
no coherent runtime support for them and allowing them through the checker
would otherwise end in a trap or linker failure:

- **Supervision trees / link-monitor / structured concurrency / tasks**: the
  production runtime modules are gated behind
  `#[cfg(not(target_arch = "wasm32"))]` in `hew-runtime/src/lib.rs`.  The
  sandbox VM separately teaches reduced M6 supervision/link/monitor semantics
  with deterministic virtual time and typed fail-closed traps; Tier 2 still
  rejects the production surface at check time to avoid undefined-symbol linker
  failures.

- **Channels (bounded subset)**: `channel.new`, sender clone/close,
  `Receiver::try_recv`, and typed `send` are available on wasm32 via the
  single-threaded queue in `hew-runtime/src/channel_wasm.rs`.
  `try_recv` preserves the native ABI contract (`None` on both empty and
  closed), while `send` fails closed by trapping with an explicit message when
  the bounded queue is full rather than silently dropping or spin-polling.

- **Blocking channel recv**: `Receiver<T>::recv`, `recv_int`, and `for await`
  over `Receiver<T>` still trap on wasm32 because the cooperative scheduler
  does not yet yield and resume when a channel is empty but still live. The
  checker rejects these operations at compile time with `BlockingChannelRecv`.

- **Blocking semaphore acquire**: `Semaphore::acquire` and
  `Semaphore::acquire_timeout` can block waiting for a permit. Native builds do
  that with condvar-style parking, but wasm32 has no cooperative permit-wait
  path yet. The checker rejects only those blocking methods and still allows
  the non-blocking semaphore subset (`new`, `try_acquire`, `release`, `count`,
  `free`).

- **Timers** (`sleep`, `sleep_until`, `#[every(duration)]`): The runtime now
  parks sleeping actors at the message boundary, re-enqueues them once the
  deadline passes, and delivers periodic handler messages through the same
  host-driven timer loop.  The checker emits a **warning** (not an error) to
  inform callers of the cooperative semantics difference.  Code after
  `sleep` in the same receive handler still executes before the park, and
  periodic dispatch depends on `hew_wasm_timer_tick(now_ms)` /
  `hew_wasm_sched_tick(...)` advancing the timer queue.

- **Streams**: The `stream` runtime module is entirely gated out on wasm32
  (`#[cfg(not(target_arch = "wasm32"))]` in `hew-runtime/src/lib.rs`).  Any
  call to a stream constructor or stream method would produce a linker error or
  undefined symbol.  Rejecting at compile time gives a clear diagnostic.
  - WASM-TODO: implement I/O stream adapters over WASI fd/socket APIs.

- **`std::net::http::http_client` / `std::net::smtp`**: these stdlib wrappers
  are still native-only today (`WASM-TODO` in the module sources).  Letting
  them through type checking on wasm32 only defers the failure to link time.
  The checker now rejects both the module helper calls and their handle methods
  (`http_client.Response.*`, `smtp.Conn.*`) with feature-specific diagnostics.
  This is distinct from any raw WASI socket support a host runtime may expose:
  Hew does not currently treat those low-level capabilities as a supported,
  portable stdlib networking surface.

- **HTTP server**: The `std::net::http` server surface is backed by native
  sockets and `tiny_http`. Its runtime symbols are unavailable on wasm32, so
  `http.listen` plus `http.Server` / `http.Request` methods are rejected at
  compile time instead of failing later in codegen or at link time.
  - WASM-TODO: design a cooperative WASI-hosted HTTP server surface.

- **TCP networking**: The `std::net` listener/connection runtime lives in the
  native transport module, which is gated out on wasm32. Rejecting `net.*`
  constructors and `net.Listener` / `net.Connection` methods keeps the checker
  fail-closed instead of leaking to undefined-symbol linker failures.
  - WASM-TODO: expose socket-backed listener/connection adapters over WASI.

- **Process execution**: The `std::process` module depends on the host OS
  process model, and its runtime module is not compiled for wasm32. Rejecting
  `process.*` helpers and `process.Child` methods at check time gives a
  feature-specific diagnostic rather than a native-symbol failure downstream.
  - WASM-TODO: define a host capability model for subprocess execution.

- **Distributed node API / remote-actor messaging**: The `Node::*` cluster API
  (`start`, `shutdown`, `connect`, `set_transport`, `load_keys`, `allow_peer`,
  `register`, `lookup`) and `RemotePid<T>::send` / `RemotePid<T>::ask` lower to
  the native mesh transport (`hew_node_api_*` and `hew_remote_pid_send` →
  `hew_actor_send_by_id`), which is gated behind
  `#[cfg(not(target_arch = "wasm32"))]` and absent from the wasm32 link set.
  Before this gate the checker admitted these on wasm32 and codegen emitted a
  module importing an undefined `env::hew_node_api_*` symbol that failed at
  instantiation (admit-then-abort). The checker now rejects the whole `Node::`
  namespace and remote messaging with `Distributed`, so distributed programs
  fail closed at check time the same way `net.*` / `quic.*` / `tls.*` already
  do. Basic single-process actors (`spawn` / `send` / `ask`) remain available.
  - WASM-TODO: decide a wasm peer transport before exposing any distributed
    surface on wasm32.

- **`std::crypto::crypto.random_bytes`**: Secure randomness is backed by
  `ring::SystemRandom`, which is native-only and absent from the wasm32 link set.
  The checker rejects `crypto.random_bytes` on wasm32 so key material generation
  fails closed instead of compiling to a non-cryptographic fallback or host
  import. WASM-TODO: plumb a secure host entropy capability such as WASI
  `random_get`.

### ⚠️ WASM-TODO (documented gap / not yet checker-gated)

Rows whose **Checker disposition** is **WASM-TODO** are intentionally *not*
claimed as supported. They remain in the matrix because the current wasm32
story is either unresolved or native-only, but Hew does not yet emit a
dedicated checker warning/error for them.

- **Raw WASI socket capability**: some WASI hosts may expose socket APIs, but
  Hew does not yet provide a stable socket abstraction that spans browser Tier 1,
  WASI Tier 2, and native builds. That is why the matrix rejects Hew's current
  high-level networking modules while keeping raw host socket capability in the
  backlog instead of marking it ✅ Pass.

---

## Generators on WASM — note

`gen fn` lowers onto the unified `llvm.coro` switched-resume continuation
substrate (`hew-runtime/src/cont.rs`), which emits identical IR on native and
wasm32. The wasm32 backend synthesizes its own `hew_gen_coro_destroy` that
routes coro-frame teardown through `llvm.coro.destroy`, so construction,
`.next()` consumption, and scope-exit teardown all release exactly one frame —
verified end-to-end under `wasmtime`
(`hew-codegen-rs/tests/exec/wasm_generator_exec.rs`).

Generator forms not yet implemented on any target are tracked in
HEW-FUTURE.md §1.6 — that is a language-surface gap, not a WASM-specific one.

Generators that depend on blocking I/O (e.g. a generator that calls
`stream.next()` internally) are additionally covered by the Streams reject
above at the point of the stream call.

---

## Checker enforcement

The `WasmUnsupportedFeature` enum in `hew-types/src/check/types.rs` is the
single source of truth for feature labels and rejection reasons.  The
`warn_wasm_limitation` and `reject_wasm_feature` methods in
`hew-types/src/check/diagnostics.rs` implement the two disposition levels.

The distinction:

```
warn_wasm_limitation  → Severity::Warning  → self.warnings
reject_wasm_feature   → Severity::Error    → self.errors
```

**Warn group** is wired in:
- `hew-types/src/check/calls.rs :: reject_if_wasm_incompatible_call` (`sleep`/`sleep_until` → `Timers` warning arm)

**Reject group** is wired in:
- `hew-types/src/check/expressions.rs :: reject_if_wasm_incompatible_expr` (scope/tasks)
- `hew-types/src/check/calls.rs :: reject_if_wasm_incompatible_call` (link/monitor/supervisor/`random_bytes`/`Node::*`)
- `hew-types/src/check/registration.rs` (supervisor actor declarations)
- `hew-types/src/check/methods.rs :: check_method_call` (stream.* / `http_client.*` / `smtp.*` / http.* / net.* / process.* / tls.* / quic.* / dns.* / os.* / `crypto.random_bytes` module calls)
- `hew-types/src/check/methods.rs` Receiver match arm (`recv` → `BlockingChannelRecv`)
- `hew-types/src/check/methods.rs` semaphore handle gate (`acquire` / `acquire_timeout` → `BlockingSemaphoreAcquire`)
- `hew-types/src/check/methods.rs` Stream / http.Server / http.Request / net.Listener / net.Connection / process.Child / tls.TlsStream / quic.QUIC* handle match arms
- `hew-types/src/check/methods.rs` RemotePid match arm (`send` / `ask` → `Distributed`)

Rows marked **WASM-TODO (not checker-gated)** currently have no dedicated
`WasmUnsupportedFeature` guard point. As of main, that bucket includes raw WASI
socket capability only. `std::net::tls`, `std::net::quic`, `std::net::dns`,
`std::os`, and `std::crypto::crypto.random_bytes` are all checker-gated.

---

## WASM-TODO backlog

These gaps are explicitly deferred and tracked here:

| Gap | Blocker | Tracking label |
|-----|---------|----------------|
| Blocking channel recv / full-queue backpressure parity | Cooperative-scheduler recv yield/resume + send backpressure beyond the bounded fail-closed slice in `channel_wasm.rs` | `WASM-TODO: channels` |
| Blocking semaphore acquire parity | Cooperative permit wait / timeout semantics for `Semaphore::acquire*` on wasm32 | `WASM-TODO: semaphore` |
| Raw socket-backed Hew networking surface | Stable cross-host socket abstraction above host-provided WASI sockets | `WASM-TODO: wasi-sockets` |
| I/O stream adapters | WASI fd/socket APIs | `WASM-TODO: streams` |
| HTTP server parity | Cooperative WASI-hosted request accept/respond runtime | `WASM-TODO: http-server` |
| TCP listener / connection parity | WASI socket-backed accept/read/write abstractions | `WASM-TODO: tcp-networking` |
| TLS client parity | wasm-capable TLS-over-sockets design plus checker/runtime classification | `WASM-TODO: tls` |
| QUIC parity | wasm-capable UDP/QUIC transport plus feature-gated runtime support | `WASM-TODO: quic` |
| DNS resolver parity | WASI-backed resolver shim; current native OS resolver is not compiled for wasm32 | `WASM-TODO: dns` |
| `std::os` parity | WASI-backed args/env/path/system shims for the current stdlib surface | `WASM-TODO: os` |
| `crypto.random_bytes` parity | Secure wasm32 entropy source and explicit capability classification | `WASM-TODO: crypto-random` |
| Process execution parity | Explicit host capability model for subprocesses | `WASM-TODO: process-execution` |
| Distributed node API / remote-actor messaging parity | wasm peer transport for the `Node::*` cluster API and `RemotePid` routing (`hew_node_api_*` is native-only) | `WASM-TODO: distributed` |
| Supervision tree restart strategies | OS-thread-free supervision design | `WASM-TODO: supervision` |
| Actor link/monitor fault propagation | OS-thread-free exit propagation | `WASM-TODO: link-monitor` |
| Structured concurrency scopes | Thread-free scope scheduler | `WASM-TODO: scope` |

> **Stackless suspension substrate (R326/R327, W6.007).** The cooperative
> yield/resume mechanism the `scope` and blocking-`recv` rows above need is now
> BUILT — an LLVM `llvm.coro.*` switched-resume continuation driven by ONE
> poll/resume executor, identical IR on native + wasm32 (see
> `docs/internal/v05-ir-ladder.md` §2.4 "Stackless suspend carrier"). It is
> **production-capable but dormant**: no source construct emits a suspend point
> yet, so these gates stay CLOSED (a relaxed gate with no readiness waker is
> fail-OPEN). The per-construct relaxation lands with the source-to-suspend flip
> + readiness waker (NEW-3); on wasm32 the `hew_sched_run` drain then drives
> resume of parked continuations cooperatively. Until then the gated behaviour
> is unchanged.

## Playground capability contract

`examples/playground/manifest.json` carries a `capabilities` object on every
entry that maps the feature disposition from this table into a machine-readable
form consumed by browser/playground tooling and the WASI e2e test suite.

```jsonc
{
  "capabilities": {
    "browser": "analysis-only",  // always — Tier 1 is analysis-only
    "wasi":    "runnable"        // or "unsupported" — see table below
  }
}
```

### Capability values

| Field | Value | Meaning |
|-------|-------|---------|
| `browser` | `"analysis-only"` | The entry can be analysed (lex/parse/typecheck) in-browser via `hew-wasm`. This value tracks the `hew-wasm` analysis crate and is invariant for all curated entries in this manifest; the sandbox VM execution target is tracked separately in `hew-lang/playground`. |
| `wasi` | `"runnable"` | The example compiles and executes correctly under `hew build --target=wasm32-wasi` (Tier 2). |
| `wasi` | `"unsupported"` | The example uses a Warn / Reject surface or relies on a documented `WASM-TODO` capability that Hew does not currently treat as runnable on WASM32. |

### Current WASI capability summary

| Example | `capabilities.wasi` | Reason |
|---------|---------------------|--------|
| `basics/*` (4 entries) | `runnable` | No WASM-limited features |
| `concurrency/actor_pipeline` | `unsupported` | Actor runtime ABI unavailable on WASI (#1821) |
| `concurrency/async_await` | `unsupported` | Actor runtime ABI unavailable on WASI (#1821) |
| `concurrency/counter_actor` | `unsupported` | Actor runtime ABI unavailable on WASI (#1821) |
| `concurrency/supervisor` | `unsupported` | Uses `supervisor`/`supervisor_child` → Reject disposition |
| `types/collections`, `types/pattern_matching`, `types/structural_bounds` | `runnable` | No WASM-limited features |
| `types/wire_types` | `unsupported` | Wire enum codec not yet lowered on WASI (#1822) |

The `WASI_CAPABILITY` table in `scripts/gen-playground-manifest.py` is the
single source of truth for these per-entry values.  Entries absent from that
table default to `"runnable"`.  The `--check` mode of that script validates
that every checked-in manifest entry carries well-formed capability metadata.

The WASI e2e test (`hew-cli/tests/wasi_run_e2e.rs`) reads `capabilities.wasi`
from the manifest to determine which examples to run vs. which to verify on the
diagnostic path, eliminating hard-coded runnable example IDs from the test
logic. Run it via `make playground-wasi-check` in codegen-capable environments
to prove the curated playground contract against the real WASI runtime path
without implying any in-browser runtime.

# Lessons Learned — Structured Reference

Source: https://github.com/hew-lang/hew/blob/main/LESSONS.md

# Lessons Learned — Structured Reference

This file is a decision aid for future Hew work. It is not a changelog.

Use it in this order:

1. Match the current change against a **core invariant** in the matching priority band.
2. Walk the **nuances** under that core; the trigger column tells you which apply.
3. Treat the **apply** column on each matching nuance as the minimum pre-merge checklist.
4. Start with the **P0** cores before applying any matching **P1** or **P2** nuances.
5. When two rules conflict, keep the stricter fail-closed, ownership-preserving, or parity-preserving rule.

## Two-level schema

A **core invariant** is the durable rule a future agent should remember even if every
nuance below it is forgotten. A **nuance** is a specific application, smell, or bug
class that has been seen in this codebase. Multiple nuances usually share one core.

Core block:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `core` | Stable short key for the core invariant. |
| `area` | Subsystem(s) where the core fires. |
| `invariant` | One-sentence durable rule. |
| `why` | The failure class the core prevents. |

Nuance row (table under the core):

| Column | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | Stable short key. **External code, docs, and specs reference these by string** — never rename a nuance id. |
| `trigger` | Smell or change pattern that should activate the nuance. |
| `apply` | Concrete check or action to take now. |
| `evidence` | Main PRs / JOURNEY workstreams that produced the nuance. |

## Priority bands

| Band | Use it for |
| --- | --- |
| `P0` | Silent wrong-code, memory safety, ownership, cleanup, or cross-language boundary risk. |
| `P1` | Parity, tests, diagnostics, toolchain, or user-surface trust. |
| `P2` | Architecture, cleanup, deduplication, and maintenance decisions that prevent repeat bugs. |

---

## P0 — Compiler/runtime correctness and boundary safety

### `boundary-fail-closed` — every cross-boundary handoff either carries the full payload or stops

- **area**: serialization, codegen, FFI, distributed surface, generated code
- **invariant**: A boundary that crosses Rust↔C++, host↔runtime, local↔remote, or generator↔repo must encode its full supported form or fail loudly with context. Silent omission, sentinel-shaped success, and emitted-but-uncounted diagnostics are bugs.
- **why**: Boundaries are where types lose their bite. Anything dropped or coerced to a sentinel becomes a silent wrong-output channel that the type system can no longer protect.

| id | trigger | apply | evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `runtime-bounds-trap-seam` | A runtime FFI entry point validates ordinary user-supplied bounds or preconditions itself instead of relying on a MIR/codegen pre-check. | Keep the check at the boundary, but route the failure through the shared trap seam (`runtime_bounds_trap` / `hew_trap_with_code`) rather than `libc::abort()`, `panic!()`, or a sentinel-shaped success. Native runtime callers must abort if `hew_trap_with_code` returns with no actor recovery context, because codegen's paired `llvm.trap` fallback is not present inside runtime functions. Classify nearby aborts before changing them: ordinary invalid input uses the trap seam; codegen-supplied metadata invariants and resource exhaustion remain distinct failure classes. Pin both actor-context isolation and main-context nonzero termination so the fix cannot become fail-open. | #2338: Vec method, bytes, and string runtime bounds failures now trap through the actor-isolating seam, with main-context exit-134 ratchets and actor-isolation fixtures. |
| `serializer-fail-closed` | A Rust-to-C++ or wire boundary must encode types, schema data, or unsupported shapes. | Reject unsupported nested forms, carry span/context through conversion, turn warning-and-skip paths into hard errors, and version or contract-test high-risk seams. | PR #812/#811/#808/#795. |
| `vec-element-width-symmetric-abi` | Adding or reclassifying a `Vec<T>` element width, constructor, method symbol, range-slice path, OR any element-ABI classification predicate (heap-owning, indirect-enum, BitCopy). | Treat the Vec element-width ABI as one contract across runtime exports, C ABI declarations, type-level method templates, HIR gates, MIR dispatch, codegen declarations/marshalling, and executable fixtures. Narrow integer and f32 values need dedicated typed symbols so push/set truncate to the storage width and get/pop sign- or zero-extend according to the Hew element type; range-slice can share one stride-generic byte-copy runtime symbol only after ownership-aware string/ptr/owned/layout paths have been selected first. Oracle lesson: behavioural/leak green is NON-EVIDENCE for ownership provers (wrong frees pass under allocator luck); the honest oracle is a `drop_plans`-level / release-call-COUNT assertion (`== 1`) per admitted AND excluded shape, with `MallocScribble` making freed-reads deterministic — NOT a presence test (`ir.contains`) or `leaks --atExit`. String `r.field`/`t.0` field-load double-free (`2026-06-19`, `fix/v06-string-field-load-double-free`): issue #37 retained fresh-PRODUCED string temps (`a + b`, `hew_vec_get_str`) but a `string` READ out of a still-live record/tuple (`RecordFieldLoad`/`TupleFieldLoad`) was emitted as a raw no-retain alias of the parent's field buffer; consumed into a sink (`hew_hashmap_insert` vacant-slot key-move, or a duplicate tuple-element read) it double-freed against the parent's own drop. The fix is TWO-SIDED and the two sides MUST land in lockstep: a codegen `hew_string_clone` retain at the field-load site REVERSES the no-retain premise, so the MIR side must ALSO (a) register the dest as a fresh `+1` producer (`string_field_load_producer_dest`) and (b) EXCLUDE it from the projection-alias taint seed (`compute_projection_alias_taint`, type-gated on the dest's `ResolvedTy` threaded as a `locals` table) so the existing `derive_cow_fresh_borrowed_owner` admits its one balancing `hew_string_drop` — exactly the `hew_vec_get_str` (`xs.get(i)`) retained-interior-load class. A codegen retain WITHOUT the MIR admission does NOT re-double-free; it INVERTS the bug into a leak (the `+1` has no drop). Scope is `string`-ONLY: non-string managed field loads (`bytes`/`Vec<T>`/nested record) are NOT retained (`cow_value_leaf_drop_symbol` returns `None`, never schedules their drop), so retaining them without a balancing drop would invert their SAFE leak too — leave them un-retained until the retain-on-share spine lands. Oracle-isolation trap: a `leaks --atExit` floor CANNOT witness this leak-inversion for a no-escape transient field read, because reading a string field SUPPRESSES the parent aggregate's own in-place field drop (the parent becomes a live operand) AND the retained value shares ONE refcounted buffer with the parent's field — so balanced vs un-balanced leaves the SAME single leaked buffer (a higher refcount, not a distinct node); that parent-field-drop leak is itself a pre-existing out-of-scope spine, equal pre/post-fix (verify by measuring the baseline SHA). Prove the no-escape balance by a `--dump-mir elab` retain==drop count (one `hew_string_drop` per field load on every exit + loop-back edge) plus a `MallocScribble` no-OVER-drop pin with an EXACT-output assertion (the parent drop and the retain drop both act on the shared buffer — a mis-balance over-decrements → sentinel abort or scribbled value), NOT a leak-node floor. Cousins: `field-alias-fail-closed`, `static-classification-vacuates-refcount-and-sanitizer`, `unclonable-leaf-fails-closed-transitively`. F-01 (`fix/v06-f01-actor-spawn-uaf`, 2026-06-23): `let t = Vec::new(); spawn Actor(field: t)` — MIR records the spawn aggregate operation as `AliasedIntoAggregate` (not `Consumed`/`MaybeConsumed`), so a classify-by-consumed-status escape scan admitted `t` as non-escaped and emitted a scope-exit drop → double-free (SIGSEGV at actor shutdown, deterministic under `MallocScribble`). One-function swap to `derive_local_collection_drop_allowed` at `hew-mir/src/lower.rs:24319` excludes `t` by finding it as a source operand of the spawn aggregate. Aggregate-into-spawn is a distinct taint class; the exhaustive source-operand scan covers it without enumerating each aggregation mode. #1942 (`fix/v06-match-vec-drop-fixpoint-hang`, 2026-06-27): the whole-value alias-propagation fixpoint that seeds these scans must be **monotone or it does not terminate** — `alias_of.insert(dl, root)` REPLACES a slot's root, so when one slot receives `Move`s from two distinct roots (a `match`/if-join result slot fed by two arms each constructing a fresh local collection) the two roots OSCILLATE, `changed` never clears, and lowering spins until SIGKILL (`hew check` hung at ~9.6s CPU on a 2-arm `Vec<i64>`-returning match — a compile HANG is worse than a clean reject). A propagation step may only ADD an entry or EVICT a conflicted one: a candidate adopting another group's root for the FIRST time (slot still self-seeded — the `let b = a;` merge) takes it once; a slot already carrying a DIFFERENT non-self root that sees a second distinct root is reachable from two groups, so EVICT it and bar re-entry (`conflicted` set). Each slot then transitions at most twice (self-seed/vacant → merged → conflicted), bounding the fixpoint at O(locals). Eviction is the conservative drop direction: an evicted slot reads as a non-member in the escape scan, so a `Move` into it EXCLUDES the source's root — fail-closed (the ambiguous group leaks, never double-frees), matching the layer-3 default. Extracted the five copies of the loop (enum/record/collection/bytes/tuple `derive_*_drop_allowed`) into one shared `propagate_whole_value_alias_roots` so every scan converges identically. Indirect-enum heap-node free (`feat/v06-drop-elaboration`, 2026-06-28, gap #46): an `indirect enum` (spec §3.7.4) node leaked, but a scope-exit drop arm ALONE could not reach 0 — the dominant leak root was UPSTREAM of any drop. The codegen eager-allocation prologue minted a `hew_alloc` node for EVERY non-parameter indirect-enum local, but move-temps (`_t = move _ctor`) and match destructure binders (`l = move mvar.payload`) immediately OVERWRITE their slot with a received pointer, orphaning the eager node — a leak no scope-exit drop can reclaim (the original pointer is gone by the time any drop runs). LESSON: when an over-eager ALLOCATION site mints storage a later instruction overwrites, the fix is at the allocation site (gate it), not (only) at the drop site; freeing the binding's resting slot never recovers the orphaned mint. Fix part 1: gate the prologue on a construction-site scan (a local written through a tag/variant place — `Move { dest: MachineTag/MachineVariant/EnumTag/EnumVariant(local) }`); under-allocating crashes loudly (use-before-alloc on the first tag GEP), never corrupts — so the conservative error allocates too FEW, surfacing immediately. Fix part 2 — the allow-set twist: indirect enums are `intent=Read` on EVERY by-value use (the move-checker treats them as borrows per `by-value-heap-params-are-borrows`), so NEITHER a return NOR a call-argument marks the binding `Consumed` — the consume-dataflow alone cannot prove sole ownership, and a return is INDISTINGUISHABLE from a borrow-pass at the `_X = move _src` MIR level. The fail-closed proof (`derive_indirect_enum_drop_allowed`): admit a binding iff its resting local (forward-propagated from a construction site through whole-value `Move`) owns a freshly-constructed node AND is NOT moved into a parent node's variant payload (`Move { dest: MachineVariant/EnumVariant{parent}, src: child }` — the parent's recursive free owns the child) AND survives the existing `returned_aggregate_members` skip + `Consumed` filter + fan-out union-find collapse. The recursive free is a synthesised `__hew_indirect_enum_free_<Enum>(ptr)` thunk: null-check, tag-dispatch, recurse into owned child indirect-enum pointers FIRST (post-order), then `hew_dealloc`; the block skeleton is appended BEFORE recursing into child thunks so a mutually-recursive `A`↔`B` pair short-circuits at the `count_basic_blocks()>0` re-entry guard instead of looping forever in synthesis (a compile-time stack overflow otherwise). Residual fail-closed leak: a node returned to the caller, whose call-result binding is not a construction site, is not admitted → leaks (tracked caller-side-ownership follow-on), never double-frees. Negative control proven: a NAMED child nested into a parent (`let left = Node(..); let t = Node(left, ..)`) frees exactly once under MallocScribble+libgmalloc (the parent's recursive free owns `left`); 4-leaf tree 19→0, single leaf 3→0, mutual `A`↔`B` chain 0; oracle `indirect_enum_drop_leak_oracle.rs`. |

| `coroutine-handle-must-be-driven-or-fail-closed` | A codegen call site emits a `build_call` to a generated function that MAY lower as an `llvm.coro` presplitcoroutine ramp (its body can carry a `sleep`/`await`/`Suspend`) — an actor `#[on(start)]`/`init`/`#[on(stop)]` lifecycle hook, a periodic handler, any new call path to a function whose suspendability varies with source. A call site to a possibly-suspending generated fn MUST drive the handle, never discard it: poll it (`hew_cont_poll`), and on Ready reclaim the frame (`hew_cont_destroy`) — on Pending PARK it so the scheduler's resume re-entry (`resume_park`/`resume_suspended_activation` via `has_live_parked_cont`) drives it to completion across every suspension, exactly the way the actor dispatch trampoline drives a suspending `receive fn`. The discriminator is the callee's LLVM return type (`ptr` = ramp, traced via `declare_function`'s `is_coroutine_function`→`ptr`-return rule to the MIR `Terminator::Suspend` carrier — NOT a name heuristic). Park ordering mirrors the dispatch suspend edge: RELEASE the actor state lock before parking (a suspended actor holding its lock deadlocks senders — FG2/R2 P0); install the actor's execution context as the current context across the ramp call so a suspend's `hew_actor_self()`-keyed readiness source (the sleep timer) arms against the RIGHT actor; ZERO-init the context carrier so a resumed `cancel_token`/pointer read is null not stack garbage. If the hook genuinely CANNOT be resumed in its context — teardown (`#[on(stop)]` runs after the actor is terminal, no activation to park into) or two sequential coroutines on one actor (suspending `init()` + `#[on(start)]`, only one continuation can park at a time) — FAIL CLOSED at compile with a clear diagnostic, never emit the discard. Cover BOTH the direct-spawn and supervised-restart lifecycle sites, on native AND wasm (the wasm scheduler is a parallel module needing its own `_park_lifecycle_cont` export under `#[cfg_attr(not(test), no_mangle)]` to avoid a native-test symbol clash), and classify any new runtime export in `jit-symbol-classification.toml`. The proving gate is a COMPILED `.hew` exec asserting the post-suspend state (the receive-path / Rust-crate suite is green over the discard — `cargo test` never runs `hew build`'s output); the memory-safety proof is a per-actor leak-slope oracle (frame reclaimed exactly once, flat slope under `MallocScribble`). | fix/v06-on-start-suspension-resume (#2269): `emit_actor_spawn_lifecycle` (`hew-codegen-rs/src/llvm.rs` ~12183) called `__on_start` with a plain `build_call` and discarded the returned coro handle; a `#[on(start)]` with `sleep(50ms)` printed `before`/`0` instead of `before`/`after`/`99` (everything after the sleep, incl. `value=99`, dropped). Cousin of `codegen-call-matches-callee-arity` and `intrinsic-stub-fail-closed-every-path` (codegen call-boundary defects the Rust suite cannot see). |
| `aggregate-abi-by-classifier-not-per-symbol` | Crossing the C-ABI boundary with an aggregate (struct/tuple/`bytes`/`#[repr(C)]`) larger than a register — declaring how it is returned or passed — OR adding a per-symbol allowlist / hand-encoded register-pair declaration / `_raw` out-pointer twin to make one symbol's aggregate ABI work on one platform. | Per-target aggregate passing is a latent-trap class: SysV/AAPCS return a ≤16-byte aggregate in a register pair while Windows x64 MSVC returns EVERY non-{1,2,4,8}-byte aggregate indirectly via a hidden `sret` pointer, and a hand-encoded `{i64,i64}`/`[2 x i64]` declaration that dodges LLVM's own ABI logic on one platform miscompiles on the other (the trap-206 / `_raw`-family origin). | `no-live-borrow-across-opaque-callback` | A runtime FFI function (`hew_rc_drop`/`hew_arc_drop`/any `hew_*` entry that owns a header before the payload) holds a live `&mut`/`&` reference INTO an allocation across a call to an opaque caller-supplied callback (a `drop_fn`/destructor/visitor `extern "C" fn`), OR reads more header fields AFTER such a call through the same reference. | The callback is opaque and may reach back into the SAME allocation (read or write), so any reference into that allocation held live across the call aliases the callback's access — undefined behaviour under both Stacked and Tree Borrows, latent until a non-null callback that touches the allocation is wired. | `recursive-admission-needs-indirection-witness` | Relaxing a type-admission gate (RcFree / collection-element / drop-derivation) to admit a recursive user type, OR adding a structural marker/heap-ownership walk over a type graph that can be self-recursive. | A recursive type is representable ONLY when a heap indirection breaks the value-size cycle: admit a cycle whose back-edge passes through a `Vec`/`HashMap`/`HashSet` (or other heap-allocated) field (`enum R { A(Vec<R>) }` — finite value size, drop terminates at the heap buffer); STILL REJECT a direct value back-edge (`enum E { V(E) }` — infinite size). The admit/reject test is whether the recursive back-edge is reached through a heap-indirecting builtin's type args (admit, the indirection is the witness) vs a direct value member (reject). Pin BOTH directions as tests — the negative (`enum E { V(E) }` rejects) is load-bearing: over-admitting pushes an infinite-size value type to codegen → unbounded layout recursion / stack overflow. SEPARATELY, ANY structural recursion over a type graph that the relaxed gate now admits MUST carry a visited-set (or depth bound) guard: a marker-derivation / heap-ownership / clone-classification walk with no guard diverges (stack overflow) the moment it meets a `Vec<Self>`-bearing type — and the overflow fires at `hew check`, not run. **The guard's key must NOT grow with the walk.** A walk that recurses THROUGH generic substitution (instantiating each level's fields with the parent's type args) and keys its visited-set on the substituted `(name, args)` pair is still fail-OPEN: a diverging polymorphic self-reference — `Wrap<T> { w: Wrap<Wrap<T>> }` — substitutes to a strictly LARGER arg vector at every level (`Wrap<i64>` → `Wrap<Wrap<i64>>` → …), so the `(name, args)` key never collides and the walk expands without bound (heap OOM, not a stack overflow). Key the bound on a NON-growing discriminator instead — the bare type NAME on the active expansion path (record the type→type edge before descending, then skip re-descent into a name already active, since its outgoing edges are already owned by the outer frame), or a hard depth bound. Keep the admission gate fail-closed for any admitted-but-not-yet-lowerable shape (e.g. a recursive enum whose nested owned-Vec field clone/drop synthesis does not exist yet): admit at the boundary ONLY what the full lowering pipeline can handle, or keep it rejected with a clear diagnostic (never a codegen-front error or overflow). | W5.016 F4 (2026-06-02): `implements_rc_free` admits an indirection-broken cycle (a `Recursive(name)` back-edge through a `Vec`/`HashMap`/`HashSet` arm) but the general `Named` walk keeps a direct value back-edge rejected. `implements_marker` gained a visited-set (`implements_marker_guarded`) — before it, a `Vec<Self>`-bearing enum overflowed the stack deriving Copy. `Vec<RedisReply>` stayed fail-closed at the owned-element gate (recursive enum-clone synthesis is a follow-on). (2) The value-type cycle detector (`hew-types/src/cycle.rs::detect_recursive_value_type_cycles`) keyed its expansion visited-set on `(name, args)` and OOM'd on `Wrap<Wrap<T>>` (8 GB+ RSS on a 3-line program) — bounded by an active-name set so the detector terminates and rejects `Wrap` as infinitely sized. |

### `checker-authority` — checker output is authoritative, downstream consumes, no re-inference

- **area**: typecheck, enrichment, serialization, codegen
- **invariant**: Whatever the checker resolves — receivers, types, generics, visibility, assignment targets, ABI choices, pattern legality — must survive the boundary into serialization and codegen. Downstream phases consume those facts; they do not rediscover them by AST fallback or span-keyed lookup.
- **why**: Re-inference at codegen time is racy with checker order and stale across function scopes, and span-keyed lookups can be absent or contradict metadata the lowering pass already tracked. Once an authority loses its monopoly, two phases disagree and silently produce wrong code.

| id | trigger | apply | evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `type-info-survival` | A later phase is tempted to re-infer receiver, type, visibility, or stdlib catalog facts that the checker already resolved; OR the checker's side-table producer is recorded at only SOME of the syntactic sites a downstream phase consumes (e.g. records inferred calls but skips the explicit-turbofish form). | Thread inferred call args, receiver authority, `Self` generics, visibility, module-aware names, and catalog-driven resolution through side tables or serialization; seed both HIR and the checker from the catalog, and fail if a downstream phase cannot see the authoritative answer. The producer must record at EVERY site the consumer reads — a per-site recording gate keyed on surface syntax (turbofish-vs-inferred) is fail-open: the skipped site starves the pipeline and trips the downstream NYI/unresolved arm, while the recorded site works, so the bug looks like a missing downstream feature when it is really a missing producer entry. The fix is to widen the producer (records unconditionally, fail-closed at the value boundary on residual inference vars), never to re-infer downstream. 'At the value boundary' means the `check_program` OUTPUT boundary, AFTER inference fully settles — NOT a guard inside the `synthesize`-time recorder: a return-type-polymorphic call (`Stack::new()` / `new_stack<T>()`, whose `T` is fixed by the expected return type) binds its type params only AFTER `synthesize` returns, when `check_against`/`expect_type` unifies the annotation, so a record-time 'all args concrete' guard is itself fail-OPEN — it drops the entry while `T` is still `Ty::Var` and re-trips the NYI arm, even though argument-driven and turbofish forms (concrete by record time) work. Snapshot the substitution representative unconditionally and let the output boundary re-resolve + prune (`validate_call_type_args_output_contract`), exactly as the record-init surface already does. Before believing a "downstream lowering is unimplemented" report, check whether the inferred-arg control already works end-to-end — if it does, the gap is the recording gate, not the lowering arm. | PR #814/#806; stdlib-resolution slice 5. F4 turbofish generic-call (2026-06-14): both generic-call application sites in `hew-types/src/check/calls.rs` passed `type_args.is_none()` as the `call_type_args` record flag, so an explicit `id<i64>(5)` was never recorded and MIR fell through to "function call NYI" — while `let y: i64 = id(5)` compiled and ran. Fixed by recording at every generic call site (`true`); the existing `record_concrete_call_type_args` inference-var guard keeps the boundary fail-closed. | `target-constant-from-threaded-arch-not-host-cfg` | A MIR/codegen value depends on the COMPILE TARGET (pointer width, ABI width, signed-MIN/-1 trap constant, shift-range bound, enum tag width) and is computed from `cfg!(target_pointer_width)`/`#[cfg(target_arch=…)]` on the COMPILER HOST, OR a classification helper returns `None`/fail-closed for a platform-sized type (`isize`/`usize`) "because the width is not knowable here". | The constant MUST derive from the target threaded through the pipeline (the checker's `wasm_target`/`pointer_width`, HIR's `TargetArch`, a MIR `PointerWidth` field on the Builder), NEVER a host `cfg!`: a cross-compile (`--target wasm32` on a 64-bit host) computing the host width emits a width-64 shift bound / `i64::MIN` guard into a 32-bit module → out-of-range shifts silently admitted and the wrong signed-MIN trap = a fail-OPEN soundness hole, invisible to a host build/test. | `per-module-type-identity` | A type/method registry, duplicate gate, or name-resolution arm keys a user/std `pub type` or `pub actor` (or its `Type::method` / receive-fn sig) by **bare name** against a single global map. | A `pub type`'s identity is `(defining-module, name)`, not bare `name`: scope the duplicate-definition gate to the current module (root/flat = `None`), so two modules may each declare a same-named type while a second declaration *within one module* still errors. Builtins stay global. Resolve a bare reference local-first; a bare name exported by 2+ imported modules is a typed `AmbiguousType` error (never silent first-wins). Critically, `fn_sigs["Type::method"]` and `TypeDef.methods` are also last-write-wins across modules — an impl body must read its return type from the module-local qualified type def (`{short}.Type`), not the bare key, or one module's `impl Trait for T` silently clobbers another's (witnessed: websocket+http both `impl ServerMethods for Server` → `expected Request, found Conn` inside websocket). The collision can be silent when the colliding sigs happen to coincide (json/toml/yaml `Value` methods all return primitives) — assert qualified resolution binds to the right def, do not trust a clean check. Shortening a module qualifier is sound for LAYOUT-KEY agreement (find the bare-registered layout) but UNSOUND for IDENTITY comparison: a `strip-known-module-prefix-then-compare-bare` canonicalization is fail-OPEN — it collapses two distinct modules' same-bare-name types (`closableerr.CloseError` vs `closableerr2.CloseError`) into one and ACCEPTS a wrong-module impl, deferring to a later codegen-front failure instead of rejecting at the type boundary. Compare DEFINING-MODULE identity (qualify a bare trait-side name against the trait's owner module via its `{module}.Trait` registry alias); never strip-then-compare-bare. The trait-side canonicalization must be SIDE-SPECIFIC: a bare name in the TRAIT DECLARATION always qualifies to the trait owner (the importer's local type names cannot change what the trait requires), while a local-shadow carve-out (keep the bare name so a local type correctly mismatches) applies ONLY to the IMPL/actual side. A SHARED local-shadow filter over both sides is itself fail-OPEN: when the importer has a local `CloseError`, it leaves the trait side's bare `CloseError` bare too, so it compares EQUAL to the impl's local type instead of the owner's required `closableerr.CloseError`, falsely accepting a wrong-module impl. And ambiguity is decided over PUBLISHED bare bindings, not over every module that EXPORTS the name: a plain `import` that exported but did not opt the name in must not contribute, or it poisons an explicit named import of the same bare name. A bare ref published by exactly one module binds to that owner's QUALIFIED identity so a sibling exporting the same bare name cannot collapse them downstream; the same fail-closed gate guards the bare record CONSTRUCTOR, not only type positions. For ALIASED imports (`import m::{ T as U }`) the published-bare map must carry SOURCE identity (`binding U -> owner.OriginalName m.T`), never reconstruct `m.U` from the binding name — reconstruction either fails closed or binds the wrong nominal type when `m` also exports a real `U`; and named-import opt-in matches by SOURCE NAME only (the alias affects only the binding, never which source export the spec selects), or a distinct export literally named `U` is falsely opted in under `U`. A SUPERTRAIT edge has a DIFFERENT resolution scope than a primary trait reference: `Base` in `trait Sub: Base` is spelled in `Sub`'s DECLARING module, so it must resolve through THAT module's import bindings (the re-export chain to the original owner), never the final importer's same-name trait — and never the local-shadow step (a declaring-module super is never the importer's local trait). When the declaring module RE-IMPORTED its super (`import other::{ Base }; trait Sub: Base`), there is no same-module `{declaring}.Base` def, so a `{declaring}.Base`-only qualifier falls back to the bare name and binds whatever `Base` the importer has — a collision-unsafe fail-OPEN that accepts a wrong-signature inherited method. Record each module's own trait imports in a `(declaring_module, binding) -> {owner}.Source` table (aliases included: `B -> other.Base`) and resolve the super edge through it; self-register the module's own pub traits so a chain terminates at the origin. Route EVERY trait reference (primary, bound, supertrait edge) through ONE resolver scoped Current-vs-Declaring, so identity is keyed by owner not bare spelling; an unresolved super then fails CLOSED against an absent method set, never accept-all. Stdlib obeys the same qualified-by-default gate — a plain `import std::…` does not expose a type bare; only genuine prelude bootstrap surfaces (always-in-scope, no user import) publish bare. The owner-qualified key must also flow to the IMPL-SIDE associated-type / default-method machinery, NOT only the conformance method-set check: the required-associated-type ENFORCEMENT, the default-associated-type collection, and the default-method registration each read `trait_defs` for the impl's `trait_bound` — keying those on the bare `tb.name` lets a same-name trait imported by a DIFFERENT module overwrite the global bare `trait_defs[name]` (last-write-wins, HashMap-order-dependent) so an impl that omits a required `type` is ACCEPTED whenever the empty same-named trait wins the write. Route them through the conformance resolver (`resolve_trait_conformance_identity` → `trait_defs_key_for_identity`, exposed as `trait_defs_key_for_bound`). EXCEPTION — the projection-binding POPULATION (`impl_assoc_type_bindings`) must STAY on the bound spelling: its `(target, trait, assoc)` key and the carrier `trait_name` that `substitute_trait_sig_for_impl` / `project_assoc_types` build are all keyed on the bound AS WRITTEN, so re-keying its `trait_defs` read on the owner-qualified identity makes the lookup SUCCEED for an aliased bound where the bare alias has no entry, writing a binding that was previously absent and firing the projection collapse asymmetrically (trait side collapses to the concrete assoc, impl side written `Self::Item` does not) — a false signature-mismatch on a sound impl. The `dyn`-trait subsystem (`apply_trait_object_bound_substitutions`, `validate_dyn_trait_bound`, the vtable-slot lookup, `actor_satisfies_handler_trait`, the dyn assoc-binding-completeness check) is internally consistent on the BARE trait name across BOTH its write side (`record_trait_impl` keys `trait_impls_set` on bare `tb.name`) and read side, so routing one member in isolation desyncs it — owner-qualifying the dyn family means moving its WRITE keys together, a separate reshape; the family probed sound under same-name + swapped-method-order collisions (verified by `hew run`, correct vtable slot). | W5.018 per-module-type-namespace (R313): cleared Conn/Value/Server/Message/ParseError/StreamPair std collisions; witnessed websocket+http both `impl ServerMethods for Server` → `expected Request, found Conn`. feat/v050-qualified-actor-identity (2026-06-10): closed the ACTOR instance end-to-end — checker tables dotted-primary (dotted key AUTHORED, never copied from the bare winner), spawn/ask identity is the `LocalPid<module.Actor>` inner name, bare refs resolve local-first with typed `AmbiguousActorReference`, every native symbol through one `$`-mangle authority (root actors stay bare = zero ABI churn). | `alloc-align-from-type-not-runtime-proxy` | A heap allocator (Arc/Rc/box/vec/any header-prefixed payload) computes its payload **alignment** (or any layout fact: size, padding) from an INCIDENTAL runtime value — the source pointer's `(addr).trailing_zeros()`, the byte `size.trailing_zeros()`, or a capped `max_align_t` guess — instead of the type's authoritative ABI alignment. | The allocation alignment MUST come from the type's real ABI alignment threaded from codegen (which knows the LLVM layout: `target_data.get_abi_alignment(&ty)`), never inferred from a runtime proxy. | `variant-detection-by-resolution` | Classifying a pattern identifier as a variant/constructor vs a fresh binding (in `let`, `match`, `if let`, `while let`), OR any name-vs-builtin classification in the checker where a syntactic heuristic (uppercase-first-letter, keyword membership) is used to decide whether a name is a binding introduction or a reference to a known construct. | Classify by RESOLUTION: a name is a variant/constructor/handler-pattern only if it resolves to a known variant, constructor, or handler in the current scope — never by a syntactic case-heuristic (uppercase-first-letter or similar).
